chapters.n: Obadiah, the shortest book in the Old Testament, is a vision about Edom, Israel’s neighbor and relative. God has sent word among the nations to rise up in battle against Edom. It likely dates soon after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587/586 BC.

f.g: The nation descended from Esau, Jacob’s twin brother, living southeast of the Dead Sea.

f.w: We have heard a rumour from the LORD

chapters.n: God declares that He will make proud Edom small and despised among the nations.
Edom’s pride has fooled it. Living in high, rocky cliffs, Edom thought no one could ever bring it down. Edom’s strongholds, like the later city of Petra, were carved into red-rock mountains.

f.w: The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee

f.g: Hebrew sela (“rock”) may also echo Sela, an Edomite stronghold.

chapters.n: Even if Edom soars like an eagle or nests among the stars, God will bring it down. No height is beyond His reach.

f.w: set thy nest among the stars

chapters.n: Thieves take only what they want, and grape pickers leave some grapes behind. But Edom will be stripped completely.

f.g: An outburst of lament in the middle of the sentence — “how you will be ruined!”

f.w: would they not leave some grapes?

chapters.n: Esau’s hidden treasures will be searched out and plundered. Edom grew rich from trade routes, but its wealth won’t stay hidden.
Edom’s own allies and friends will betray it, setting a trap even while sharing its table. The nation known for wisdom will not see it coming.
Edom was famous for its wise men, but God will remove their wisdom and understanding.

f.w: the wise men out of Edom

chapters.n: Edom’s warriors will be terrified, and its people cut down.

f.g: A region in Edom, home of Eliphaz, one of Job’s friends.

chapters.n: The core charge: Edom committed violence against its own brother, Jacob. Betraying family deserves shame.
When foreigners (the Babylonians) captured Jerusalem and gambled over its spoils, Edom stood by and acted just like one of the invaders.
Eight times Obadiah says “you should not have.” You should not have gloated over your brother’s disaster, celebrated Judah’s ruin, or bragged in their distress.

f.w: thou shouldest not have looked on

chapters.n: Nor should Edom have entered Jerusalem’s gates to gloat and loot while the city suffered. The repeated “day of their calamity” stresses how heartless this was.
Worst of all, Edomites stood at the crossroads to cut off refugees and handed survivors over to the enemy.

f.g: A fork in the road or mountain pass — where fugitives could be caught.

chapters.n: The day of the Lord is near for all nations. A key principle: what you do to others will come back on you.

f.w: as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee

chapters.n: As Edom drank in celebration on God’s holy mountain, so all nations will drink the cup of God’s judgment until they stagger and vanish.
In contrast, Mount Zion will be a place of rescue and holiness, and Jacob’s descendants will reclaim their inheritance.

f.w: upon mount Zion shall be deliverance
the house of Jacob shall possess their possessions

chapters.n: Jacob and Joseph’s houses will be like fire, and Esau’s house like dry straw — consumed completely.

f.g: The northern tribes; here all Israel is reunited.

chapters.n: Israel’s people will spread out to reclaim surrounding lands: Edom, Philistia, Ephraim, Samaria, and Gilead.

f.g: People of the Negev, Judah’s southern desert.
Land east of the Jordan River.

chapters.n: Exiles from both Israel and Jerusalem will return and resettle the land as far north as Zarephath and throughout the southern towns.

f.g: A distant place of exile, often identified with Sardis in Asia Minor; later Jewish tradition used the name for Spain.

chapters.n: Deliverers will rise on Mount Zion, and the kingdom will belong to the Lord. Latter-day Saints see in “saviours on mount Zion” those who do temple work for the dead, becoming saviors for others through Christ.

f.w: saviours shall come up on mount Zion
the kingdom shall be the LORD's
